opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so what I find really exciting about PromptBreeder is that it brings together two ideas I've cared about for a long time: open-ended, evolutionary search on one hand, and large language models on the other. And it turns out they fit together remarkably well.

The basic setup is simple. You have a population of prompts for some task, say solving grade-school math problems, and you evolve that population over time. You evaluate each prompt by how well the model does on the task with it, keep the fitter ones, and mutate them to produce new variants. What's different from classic genetic algorithms is the mutation operator. In traditional evolutionary computation you'd flip bits or swap tokens at random, which for natural language would mostly produce gibberish. Here the language model itself is the mutation operator. You give it something like "Here's a prompt, make a variation of it" or "Rephrase this instruction in a way that might help a student," and it produces a semantically meaningful mutation. So you get the exploratory power of evolution while staying in the space of sensible language.

The part I find most intellectually interesting is the self-referential aspect. In PromptBreeder we don't just evolve the task prompts. We also evolve the mutation prompts, the instructions that tell the LLM how to mutate the task prompts. So the system is improving not only its solutions but also the way it searches for solutions. That loop of improving how you improve feels like a small but concrete step toward systems that can bootstrap their own capabilities without a human carefully hand-engineering every piece.

It was also humbling in a way. People had spent a lot of effort hand-crafting prompting strategies like "Let's think step by step" or Plan-and-Solve, and PromptBreeder could discover prompts that beat them on benchmarks like GSM8K. Some of the evolved prompts are quite odd. They're not what a human would write, yet they work. That says something about how little we understand what these models actually respond to, and about the value of letting search explore that space for us rather than relying on intuition.

More broadly, I see it as one example of a bigger theme: language models give us really powerful priors over what is interesting or plausible, and evolutionary or open-ended search gives us a way to keep generating novelty on top of those priors. Combining the two is, I think, one of the most promising directions toward more autonomous, self-improving systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, what I find really exciting about PromptBreeder is that it's essentially an open-ended, self-referential system operating in the space of natural language. For a long time, people have been doing prompt engineering by hand, right? You sit there and you try "let's think step by step" or you try some other phrasing, and you see what works. And that's a very manual, very brittle process. So the obvious idea is: can we automate this? Can we have a search process that discovers good prompts for us?

And the natural way to do that is evolutionary search. You have a population of prompts, you evaluate them on some downstream task, you keep the ones that work well, and then you mutate them to generate new candidates. That part alone is interesting, but it's not the part I find most fascinating.

The part I find most fascinating is that we use the language model itself as the mutation operator. So instead of having some hand-coded way of changing a prompt, you ask the LLM to rewrite it, to produce a variation of it. And then the question becomes: well, how do you tell the model to mutate things? You give it a mutation prompt. And now you realize that the mutation prompt is also just a piece of text, so you can evolve that too. So you end up with this self-referential loop where the system is not only improving the task prompts, but it's improving the way it improves the task prompts.

And I think this connects to a much deeper theme in my research, which is open-endedness. If you look at biological evolution, or at human culture, the mechanisms that generate novelty are themselves subject to change. Evolution evolved evolvability, in a sense. And language is this incredibly rich, compositional substrate where you can express almost anything, including instructions about how to modify instructions. So natural language becomes the medium for a self-improving search process, with the language model as the engine that proposes variations and the task as the selection pressure.

What was really striking to us empirically is that this just works. You end up with prompts that outperform the hand-crafted ones, and often they look nothing like what a human would have written. Sometimes they're a bit weird, honestly. But that's exactly the point. The search finds things in that space that we wouldn't have thought of, because we have very strong priors about what a "reasonable" prompt looks like, and the evolutionary process doesn't share those priors.

So for me it's a small but concrete demonstration of something I think is going to be very important: using LLMs as components in open-ended, self-referential search processes, where the thing being improved and the thing doing the improving are made of the same stuff, which is language.

r001.rationale: The response calls PromptBreeder an open-ended, self-referential system operating in natural language and describes evolutionary search over prompts.

r002.rationale: It explains that the mutation prompt is also text and can be evolved, improving how the system improves task prompts.

astra-6.text:
What I find particularly interesting is that language becomes both the thing you’re optimizing and the mechanism for producing variations. You have a population of task prompts, evaluate how well they perform, and then use a language model to generate new candidates. Those mutations can be meaningful changes in strategy, rather than just random changes to a string.

And PromptBreeder takes that a step further: it also evolves the mutation prompts—the instructions that tell the model how to change a task prompt. So the search can improve not only the solutions, but also how it searches for solutions. That’s the self-referential aspect I find exciting.

Of course, you still need a useful fitness signal. But within that constraint, you can discover instructions that you might not have thought to write yourself. It turns prompt engineering into an open-ended search over ways of eliciting capabilities from the model.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find really interesting is that language is both the thing being evolved and the mechanism for producing variation. You have a population of task prompts, and you can ask the language model to modify those prompts, then evaluate how well the new versions perform.

But PromptBreeder goes a step further: it also evolves the mutation prompts—the instructions that tell the model how to change a task prompt. So you're searching not just for a good instruction, but for better ways of discovering good instructions.

And unlike a random mutation in a conventional evolutionary algorithm, a mutation here can be quite meaningful. The model can rephrase something, introduce a different strategy, or suggest breaking a problem down. You're using the model's existing knowledge to generate variation, while selection tells you whether that variation actually helps. That combination of open-ended language and an empirical fitness signal is what I find particularly exciting.
